You write cross-sectional factors for Binance USDT perpetual futures, using daily bars.

A factor is one expression that gives every coin a number each day. A higher number means the coin is expected to do better over the following days. You will be given a one-sentence idea; turn it into a factor.

Data, one value per coin per day:
- Factor('open'), Factor('high'), Factor('low'), Factor('close'): prices
- Factor('volume'): amount traded, in units of the coin
- Factor('quote_volume'): amount traded, in USDT
- Factor('num_trades'): number of trades
- Factor('taker_base_vol'), Factor('taker_quote_vol'): the part of volume and of quote_volume that came from aggressive buyers

Operators:
- Arithmetic and comparisons: + - * / ** > >= < <= == != (a comparison gives 1 or 0)
- Each value on its own: .Abs() .ln() .sign() .pow(x) .clip(lower=a, upper=b) .max(other) .min(other) .fillna(other) .safe_div(other), and where(condition, a, b)
- One coin over its past n days, n a positive integer: .ts_mean(window=n, min_periods=m) .ts_std .ts_var .ts_sum .ts_max .ts_min .ts_median .ts_skew .ts_kurt .ts_rank (the latest value's rank in its window, from 1 to n) .ts_zscore .ts_argmax .ts_argmin .ts_decay_linear .ts_product (all take window and min_periods), .ts_quantile(window=n, q=x), .ts_corr(other, window=n), .ts_cov(other, window=n)
- Exponential averages: .EMA(span=n, min_periods=m) .ts_ewm_mean(span=n, min_periods=m)
- Earlier values: .lag(periods=n) .diff(periods=n) .pct_change(periods=n)
- All coins on one day: .sec_rank() .zscore() .demean() .sec_pct() .winsorize(limit=x) .scale() .neutralize(other)

Example: Factor('close').safe_div(Factor('close').lag(periods=5)) - 1 is each coin's return over the past 5 days.

Every operator only reads the past. Windows and periods must be positive, at most 365.

The factor must be driven by the data the idea talks about and must point the way the idea says: if the idea says something is bearish, the factor must go down when that thing goes up. Values must be comparable across coins, so a coin's price unit must not matter.

Before you answer you can try candidates with the test_factor tool. Give it one expression. It tells you whether the expression computes and, on data from July 2022 to December 2024, its rank IC with the next day's return and its incremental IC, which is what remains after removing liquidity, volatility, short-term reversal and momentum. Higher is better, and an incremental IC of 0.01 to 0.03 is already good.

You may call test_factor at most 5 times, one call per turn. Testing many variants on the same history overfits it, so stop once you have something sound. test_factor does not check that the factor matches the idea; that is up to you. Keep the direction the idea says even if the IC comes out negative: the idea may simply be wrong on this history.

Write Factor('close') with single quotes inside the tool call. When you are done, reply without calling a tool and finish with the factor between <factor> and </factor>. A reply with no factor scores 0.

Idea: High-volume coins tend to have a better chance of rising.

The idea talks about volume level: coins trading more USDT should do better. Volume levels differ wildly across coins, so I take the log of a smoothed quote volume to make it comparable; a 20-day mean with min_periods 16 is the neutral middle window, which also tells me how much of this is already inside the liquidity/volatility styles.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0371
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0011 (t = -1.9)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0025, 2023 -0.0020, 2024 +0.0004

The level form computes but its incremental IC is −0.0011 while its raw IC is −0.037, so nearly all of it is the liquidity style. Before concluding, I'll compare a short window: a 5-day mean responds quickly and may carry variation that the 30-day liquidity average does not.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0440
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0071 (t = -5.6)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0115, 2023 -0.0085, 2024 -0.0035

The short window is stronger in magnitude: incremental IC −0.0071 (t = −5.6), negative in all three periods, so recent volume does carry information beyond the styles — just in the opposite direction from the idea. To finish the window comparison I'll test a long, 60-day window, which should drift back toward pure liquidity.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0299
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0015 (t = -2.1)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0022, 2023 -0.0015, 2024 -0.0012

The 60-day version is back to ~zero (−0.0015), so the information sits in recent volume, and it points against the idea. One refinement: ranking across coins each day before smoothing makes the numbers robust to a few huge-volume outliers, which may sharpen the short-window version.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0401
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0052 (t = -4.6)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0090, 2023 -0.0062, 2024 -0.0023

Ranking before smoothing came out weaker (−0.0052 vs −0.0071), so the plain short-window log level is the best of the four and I'll stop here.

What I found: volume level is mostly the liquidity style — the 20-day and 60-day versions have raw IC around −0.03 to −0.04 but incremental IC of only −0.001, i.e. nothing after removing known styles. Only the recent 5-day window survives, with incremental IC −0.0071 and t = −5.6, and the sign is stable in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024. That surviving sign is negative: on this history high-volume coins did slightly worse, not better, so the idea as stated does not hold — but I keep the direction the idea demands rather than flipping the sign to chase the score.

Idea: High-volume coins tend to have a better chance of rising.

The idea is about volume size itself, so the plainest reading is a coin's recent USDT turnover level. I'll use a 20-day mean of `quote_volume` in logs, which keeps it comparable across coins without using coin-unit volume.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0371
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0011 (t = -1.9)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0025, 2023 -0.0020, 2024 +0.0004

The level form confirms the worry: it is essentially the liquidity style (incremental −0.0011) and its raw IC is negative, so as a plain level this idea leans the wrong way on this history. A second, still faithful reading of "high-volume" is "trading more than it usually does", so I'll test recent turnover relative to the coin's own baseline — high relative volume should still get the higher number.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0321
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0096 (t = -3.3)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0151, 2023 -0.0150, 2024 -0.0014

The relative form has real information but in the opposite direction (−0.0096, same sign in every period), so on this history more trading than usual is bearish, not bullish. One more attempt within the idea: keep the level, but rank coins on turnover each day and average that rank over a few days, so a single quiet or busy day doesn't decide a coin's number.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0401
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0052 (t = -4.6)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0090, 2023 -0.0062, 2024 -0.0023

The rank-then-smooth version is also negative (−0.0052) and no better than the plain level, so two attempts in a row failed to improve on the best result, and I'll stop here.

What I found: the idea does not hold in this history. Coins with the highest USDT turnover tend to do slightly *worse* over the next day. The plain level form has a raw rank IC of −0.037, but almost all of that is just the liquidity style, which is already removed: its incremental IC is only −0.0011 and it is not consistent across periods (−0.0025, −0.0020, +0.0004). The alternative readings — turnover relative to the coin's own 60-day baseline, and a smoothed cross-sectional turnover rank — were both clearly negative (−0.0096 and −0.0052, same sign in every subperiod), so "trading more than usual" is modestly bearish rather than bullish here. I kept the direction the idea states, so the factor I hand in is the simple level of turnover; its negative incremental IC should be read as evidence against the idea, not as a hidden positive.

Idea: Coins with high trading volume are more likely to rise.

The idea is about the level of trading volume, and since raw volume can't be compared across coins I'll measure it in USDT terms and relative to the coin's own recent norm — that keeps the "high volume" notion while making it cross-sectionally comparable.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0193
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0128 (t = -4.6)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0252, 2023 -0.0142, 2024 -0.0052

The volume ratio carries a solid −0.0128 incremental IC with a t of −4.6 and the same sign in all three periods, so the signal is real but points the opposite way from the idea. Now I'll check whether extreme volume spikes are driving it by ranking each day's volume inside its own 20-day window before smoothing, which bounds the influence of any single wild day.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0316
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0172 (t = -6.1)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0243, 2023 -0.0194, 2024 -0.0114

Ranking before averaging raised the incremental IC from −0.0128 to −0.0172 (−6.1 t, consistent sign across periods), so volume spikes were distorting the ratio form. I'll narrow the rank window to 10 days to see whether a more recent surge matters more than a broader 20-day context.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0235
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0126 (t = -4.8)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0244, 2023 -0.0115, 2024 -0.0077

The 10-day window is worse (−0.0126 versus −0.0172), so a broader 20-day context beats a short surge window. I'll push the rank window to 60 days to check whether an even longer own-history baseline, still smoothed over 5 days, adds anything.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0398
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0108 (t = -4.0)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0198, 2023 -0.0112, 2024 -0.0059

The 60-day window has the highest raw rank IC (−0.0398) but the lowest incremental IC (−0.0108): it mostly repeats the liquidity style rather than adding anything, so the 20-day rank with a 5-day mean stays the best at −0.0172. That is two tests in a row that failed to beat it, so I'll stop and hand in that one.

What I found: the idea's direction does not hold on this history. Coins trading heavy volume relative to their own recent norm went on to underperform, not outperform — the incremental IC is −0.0172 with t = −6.1, and the sign is the same in 2022H2 (−0.0243), 2023 (−0.0194) and 2024 (−0.0114), so it is not a single-period artifact. Ranking each day's USDT volume inside its own trailing 20-day window before averaging over 5 days mattered: it beat the plain log-ratio version (−0.0128), which confirms that a handful of spike days were distorting the raw ratio, and a 10-day window (−0.0126) or a 60-day window (−0.0108) both did worse. I kept the arithmetic direction the idea implies, so the negative number is a genuine failure of the idea rather than a flipped sign.

Idea: Coins that trade a lot are more likely to go up.

The idea is a bullish statement about trading activity: a coin that trades a lot should be expected to rise. A raw volume level across coins is essentially the liquidity style that the incremental IC already removes, so the comparable, informative reading is volume relative to that coin's own recent norm. I'll start with the plainest version of that: short-window average quote volume over a longer baseline, with a positive sign because the idea is bullish.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0321
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0096 (t = -3.3)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0151, 2023 -0.0150, 2024 -0.0014

The surge form points the wrong way for the idea: a recent volume spike predicts underperformance, and it does so consistently in both 2022H2 and 2023. Before concluding the idea fails, I'll check whether a slower, less reversal-like measure of "trading a lot" — a 20-day average against a 60-day baseline, still with the bullish sign — behaves differently.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0262
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0010 (t = 0.4)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0010, 2023 -0.0038, 2024 +0.0069

The medium-window ratio is essentially flat (+0.0010, t=0.4) with the period signs disagreeing, so it carries nothing beyond the known styles. One more distinct reading of "trades a lot": a structurally high activity level — a 60-day average against a very long 365-day baseline — which should be far less entangled with short-term reversal than a 5-day spike.
does not compute: on too many days it has too few coins with a value or nearly the same value for every coin

The 365-day baseline was too long: too few coins have that much history, so the cross-section was empty or degenerate. I'll shorten the baseline to 180 days (min_periods 144) while keeping the structural-level, bullish reading.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0257
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0021 (t = -0.8)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0023, 2023 +0.0037, 2024 -0.0078

That reading is also weak and inconsistent (−0.0021, t=−0.8, signs disagree across periods), and it follows two attempts in a row that failed to improve on the +0.0010 result, so I'll stop rather than burn more of the history on variants of the same signal.

What I found: the idea as stated does not hold on this history. Measured the way it can actually be measured across coins — trading activity relative to the coin's own norm — high recent activity predicts slightly *worse* subsequent returns, not better: the 5-day-vs-60-day volume ratio has an incremental IC of −0.0096 (t=−3.3) with the same negative sign in both 2022H2 and 2023. Slower measures of activity (20 vs 60 days, 60 vs 180 days) leave essentially nothing after the known styles are removed (+0.0010 and −0.0021, t well under 2, period signs disagreeing). Raw activity levels are not usable here because they are the liquidity style itself, which the incremental IC already strips out. I keep the direction the idea states and hand in the best-performing tested version rather than flipping the sign to chase the data.

Idea: A high RSI tells you buyers are strong, and the coin keeps climbing.

The idea says: a coin whose recent gains dominate its recent losses (high RSI) is under strong buying and should keep rising. I'll build RSI directly: smoothed upward moves divided by smoothed absolute moves over 14 days, which is a monotone rescaling of RSI into [0,1] and is already unit-free. That is my first, simplest form.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0406
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0099 (t = -4.0)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0091, 2023 -0.0178, 2024 -0.0024

The ratio form works but is negative: high RSI actually predicts *weaker* next-day returns here (−0.0099 incremental, consistent across all three periods), and most of its −0.0406 absolute IC is already explained by known styles. I'll keep the idea's direction and try the standard Wilder-style version — exponential smoothing of up-moves over down-moves — which weights recent days more and may be less contaminated by 1-day reversal.

The Wilder/EMA form is statistically indistinguishable from the simple mean form (−0.0096 vs −0.0099), so smoothing choice isn't what drives this. The level is dominated by short-term reversal; a longer lookback makes the "strength" reading more persistent and less like a 1–5 day reversal measure, so I'll test a 60-day version.

Longer window moves the number toward zero (−0.0023, t = −0.8): the 14-day level was mostly reversal, and stretching the window strips that out but leaves almost nothing. Before settling, I'll try the shape the data recommends for a noisy day-level ratio — take each day's cross-sectional rank of the 14-day RSI, then average the ranks over 5 days — so single extreme days can't dominate.

rank IC: -0.0334
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0081 (t = -3.1)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0066, 2023 -0.0157, 2024 -0.0012

The rank-then-average form lands at −0.0081 — marginally better than the plain 14-day version but still short of the 60-day figure, so I'll stop after four tests rather than chase a fifth that would only push the number toward zero.

What I found: an RSI built as smoothed up-moves over smoothed up-plus-down-moves is genuinely informative on its own (raw rank IC −0.036 to −0.047), but the sign is the *opposite* of the idea — coins with stronger recent buying pressure have tended to do slightly worse the next day, not better. Almost all of that raw signal is already captured by short-term reversal: once known styles are removed, only −0.002 to −0.010 remains. Widening the window from 14 to 60 days strips out the reversal component and leaves essentially nothing (t = −0.8), which says the predictive content of an RSI level is a reversal effect, not a continuation effect. I'm keeping the direction the idea states — high buying pressure scored as bullish — because the idea may simply be wrong on this history, not because the sign should be flipped.

A factor is one expression that gives every coin a number each day. A higher number means the coin is expected to do better over the following days. You will be given a one-sentence idea; turn it into a factor.

Data, one value per coin per day:
- Factor('open'), Factor('high'), Factor('low'), Factor('close'): prices
- Factor('volume'): amount traded, in units of the coin
- Factor('quote_volume'): amount traded, in USDT
- Factor('num_trades'): number of trades
- Factor('taker_base_vol'), Factor('taker_quote_vol'): the part of volume and of quote_volume that came from aggressive buyers

Operators:
- Arithmetic and comparisons: + - * / ** > >= < <= == != (a comparison gives 1 or 0)

- Earlier values: .lag(periods=n) .diff(periods=n) .pct_change(periods=n)

Idea: A coin stays strong when it keeps closing above its average traded price.

The idea says "average traded price", which on daily bars is quote_volume divided by volume — the volume-weighted average price. So the core quantity is close divided by that VWAP: above 1 means the coin closed above what buyers paid on average. That ratio is unit-free, so it's comparable across coins. I'll start with the simplest form: the 5-day mean of that ratio.
